headline: Sliding windows, list internals and CDNs: moving fast through data and around the world
intro: Today you learn the sliding window, one of the most common patterns for substring and subarray questions. The Java track opens up ArrayList and LinkedList, the design track adds a CDN to serve content close to users, and the AI track shows how to debug with AI without losing control.
connections: The sliding window (Coding) only re-processes what enters and leaves, just as a CDN edge (Design) only fetches what it does not already hold.
Window code reads s.charAt(i) by index, fast in contiguous memory; the same locality is why ArrayList beats LinkedList (Java).
The 'abba' bug (AI) is today's sliding-window edge case: left must never move backwards (Coding).

dsa.title: Sliding window
dsa.why: Sliding window questions about substrings and subarrays are extremely common at Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters is one of the most asked Medium problems anywhere, and Longest Repeating Character Replacement tests whether you really understand when a window is valid.
dsa.builds_on: Day 4: subarrays and prefix sums. Days 7–8: two pointers.
dsa.next: Day 10 adds frequency maps inside the window and the minimum-window technique.

subtopics.title: Fixed vs variable windows
subtopics.in_one_line: A window is a range [left, right] that slides; fixed windows keep their size, variable windows grow and shrink.

When

blocks.text: **Analogy:** a train window moving along a platform. You only look at the people in the window; as it moves, one person enters on the right and one leaves on the left. You update what you know instead of recounting everyone.

subtopics.title: Expand and shrink
subtopics.in_one_line: Move right to grow the window; while it breaks the rule, move left to shrink it.

blocks.title: Why it is O(n)
blocks.text: Each index enters the window once (right++) and leaves at most once (left++), so the total work is at most 2n steps, even though there is a while inside the for.

subtopics.title: Tracking what is inside the window
subtopics.in_one_line: Keep a small summary (counts, last positions, max frequency) that updates in O(1) per step.

head: Question
What to track
rows: Set of characters, or last index of each

blocks.title: Signal check
blocks.text: Sliding window needs the window to stay 'monotonic': growing it can only make it more invalid. With negative numbers and sums, that breaks, so use prefix sums (Day 4) instead.

problems.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problems.statement: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
how_to_think: Understand: substring means contiguous; characters can be letters, digits, symbols, spaces.
Brute force: check every substring for repeats. O(n³), or O(n²) with a set per start.
Improve: a window that never contains a repeat. When s[right] is already inside, move left just past its previous position.
hints: Store each character's last index. If it is inside the window (≥ left), jump left to lastIndex + 1.

approach: If lastSeen[c] ≥ left, set left = lastSeen[c] + 1.
lastSeen[c] = right; best = max(best, right − left + 1).
solution.space: O(1): a fixed 128-slot array (O(k) for a map of k distinct characters)

alternatives.name: Window with a HashSet, shrink one by one

followups.q: Why Math.max(left, …) and not just lastSeen[c]?
followups.a: The previous copy of c may be to the left of the current window; jumping to it would move left backwards and re-include repeats.

followups.q: What if the string is Unicode?
followups.a: Use a HashMap<Character, Integer> (or code points) instead of int[128].

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
problems.statement: Given a string s of uppercase English letters and an integer k, you may change at most k characters to any other uppercase letter. Return the length of the longest substring containing the same letter after these changes.
how_to_think: Understand: a window is fine if it can be made all one letter with at most k changes.
Key fact: changes needed = window length − count of its most frequent letter.
Window: grow right; if length − maxFreq > k, shrink left by one.
hints: How many changes does a window need to become all one letter?
Track counts[26] and maxFreq. You never need to decrease maxFreq: only a bigger maxFreq can give a longer answer.

approach: For each right: counts[s[right]]++; maxFreq = max(maxFreq, that count).
If (right − left + 1) − maxFreq > k: counts[s[left]]--, left++.

followups.q: Why is it fine that maxFreq is never decreased?
followups.a: The answer only grows when a window has a higher maxFreq. A stale, too-high maxFreq can keep the window from shrinking, but never makes best larger than a real valid window.

followups.q: Why if instead of while here?
followups.a: Each step adds one character, so at most one removal is needed to keep the window size from growing; the window slides at a fixed size until a better maxFreq appears.

interview_qa.q: When do you use a sliding window?
interview_qa.a: For contiguous subarrays or substrings where you want the longest, shortest or count meeting a condition, and growing the window only moves it toward invalid. You keep a summary of the window and update it as both ends move.

interview_qa.q: Why is a sliding window O(n) when it has a loop inside a loop?
interview_qa.a: Each element is added once when right passes it and removed at most once when left passes it, so the total number of steps is at most 2n.

interview_qa.q: What do you store to detect repeats in a substring window?
interview_qa.a: Either a set of characters currently in the window, or a map of each character's last index so left can jump straight past the repeat.

takeaways: Window = [left, right]; grow with right, shrink with left.
Each index enters and leaves once: O(n).
Keep an O(1)-update summary of the window.
Negative numbers usually break the window; use prefix sums.

interview_angle.asked_at: Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft phone screens and onsites; bank online tests
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters" and "…with at most k replacements"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Name the pattern, state what makes the window invalid, what you track inside it, and justify O(n) with the 'enters once, leaves once' argument.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Restarting from scratch at each index (O(n²)); off-by-one in window length (right − left + 1); shrinking with if instead of while.

java.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList: how they work inside
java.why: "ArrayList vs LinkedList" is asked in nearly every Java interview, and the textbook answer ('LinkedList is faster for inserts') is often wrong in practice. Interviewers at banks and Amazon reward candidates who explain the internals and real-world performance.

subtopics.title: LinkedList inside
subtopics.in_one_line: A chain of nodes, each holding a value and pointers to the previous and next node.

head: Operation

LinkedList
rows: O(n): walk from the nearer end

blocks.title: The practical truth
blocks.text: Inserting in the middle of a LinkedList still needs O(n) to walk there. And arrays are stored contiguously, so the CPU cache makes ArrayList faster in almost all real workloads. Use ArrayDeque for queues.

subtopics.title: When to use which
subtopics.in_one_line: Default to ArrayList; LinkedList almost never.

head: Need
Choose
rows: Many inserts at the front only
Insert/remove while iterating with a ListIterator
LinkedList can help, but measure first

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: If you load large result sets into memory in a Spring Boot or batch job, an ArrayList sized up front, or streaming rows instead of holding them all, matters more than any LinkedList trick. That is a realistic performance story.

interview_qa.q: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList?
interview_qa.a: ArrayList is a resizable array: O(1) index access and amortised O(1) append, but O(n) inserts in the middle. LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(1) at the ends but O(n) index access and much more memory per element. In practice ArrayList is faster for almost everything because of memory locality.
When the backing array is full, it creates a new array about 1.5 times larger and copies the elements. That copy is O(n), but it happens rarely, so appends are amortised O(1).

interview_qa.q: Is LinkedList faster for inserting in the middle?
interview_qa.a: Only the link change is O(1); finding the position is O(n). Combined with poor cache locality, it is usually slower than ArrayList's shift in real benchmarks.
Most operations are O(1) and an occasional one is expensive, but averaged over many operations the cost per operation is constant.

takeaways: ArrayList = resizable array; grows ~1.5× with a copy.
LinkedList = nodes with prev/next pointers; heavy on memory.
Default to ArrayList; use ArrayDeque for queues.
Amortised O(1): rare expensive steps averaged out.

interview_angle.asked_at: Core-Java rounds at UBS, Morgan Stanley and Nomura; Amazon and Microsoft Java checks
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "ArrayList vs LinkedList — when would you use each?", "How does ArrayList resize?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Give the internals, the Big-O table, and the practical point about memory locality and walking cost; conclude 'ArrayList by default, ArrayDeque for queues'.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Claiming LinkedList is faster for middle inserts without mentioning the walk; not knowing the growth factor; forgetting memory overhead.

design.title: CDNs: serving content close to users
design.why: Any design with images, video or a global user base needs a CDN, and interviewers at Google, Meta, Amazon and Netflix-style companies expect you to add one and explain cache keys, TTLs and invalidation. It is caching (Days 7–8) at internet scale.
design.builds_on: Day 2: DNS and HTTP. Days 7–8: caching, TTLs and invalidation.
design.next: Day 10 moves to the data layer: SQL vs NoSQL.

subtopics.title: What a CDN is
subtopics.in_one_line: A network of servers around the world that keep copies of your content close to users.

items.label: DNS
items.note: Points to the nearest CDN edge

items.label: Origin (your servers)
items.note: Miss: edge fetches once, then caches

blocks.text: Without a CDN, a user in Mumbai fetching from a server in Virginia pays about 200 ms per round trip. With a nearby edge, the same file arrives many times faster, and your servers barely see the traffic.

subtopics.title: What to put on a CDN
subtopics.in_one_line: Static files always; some API responses with care.

blocks.title: From your JPMorgan work
blocks.text: For an internal finance web app the CDN may not matter much, but its static frontend assets (JavaScript bundles for a pivot UI) could be served from S3 behind CloudFront. Saying when a CDN is not worth it is also a strong answer.

interview_qa.q: What is a CDN and why use it?
interview_qa.a: A globally distributed cache for content, mostly static files. It reduces latency by serving from a nearby edge, cuts load and bandwidth on origin servers, and absorbs traffic spikes.

interview_qa.q: How do you update a file that is cached on a CDN?
interview_qa.a: Best: change its URL with a version or content hash, so new pages reference the new file and the old one simply expires. Otherwise purge it, which takes time to propagate.

interview_qa.q: Would you cache API responses on a CDN?
interview_qa.a: Only public, non-personal responses that can tolerate short staleness, with a short TTL and the right cache key. Never personalised data.

takeaways: CDN = caches at the edge, close to users.
Great for static files and video; careful with APIs; never personal data.
Pull CDNs fetch from origin on a miss.
Version file names instead of purging.

resources.title: Cloudflare Learning: What is a CDN?

interview_angle.asked_at: Google, Meta, Amazon and media-heavy startups; any design with images or global users
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "Users in Asia say the site is slow" or "How do you serve images for 100 million users?"
interview_angle.strong_answer: Add a CDN in front of object storage, explain pull on miss, long TTLs with versioned URLs, and keep personalised data off it.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Putting personal data on a CDN; relying on purges for every release; forgetting the origin still needs to handle misses.

ai.title: AI-assisted debugging
ai.why: Debugging unfamiliar code is now a named part of AI-enabled interview rounds at Meta and Google. Using AI well while debugging means giving it the failing input and expected output, and checking its explanation, not asking it to 'fix my code'.
ai.builds_on: Day 7: verifying AI output. Day 8: AI-generated test cases.
ai.next: Day 10 explains embeddings: how AI represents meaning as numbers.

subtopics.title: A debugging method that works with or without AI
subtopics.in_one_line: Reproduce, isolate, explain, fix, add a test.

items: **Reproduce:** find the smallest input that fails.
**Isolate:** trace the variables by hand or with prints to find the first wrong value.
**Explain:** say in one sentence why it goes wrong.
**Fix:** change the smallest thing that addresses the cause.
**Test:** add the failing input as a permanent test.

subtopics.title: How to ask AI for debugging help
subtopics.in_one_line: Give code, the failing input, expected and actual output, and ask for the cause before the fix.

items.title: Weak
points: You learn nothing and may get new bugs

items.title: Strong
points: "Input "abba" gives 3, expected 2. Here is the code. Explain the cause in one sentence before suggesting a fix."
AI focuses on the real bug
You can check its explanation against your trace

subtopics.title: Today's exercise
subtopics.in_one_line: Debug a broken sliding window with and without AI.

items: Take your Longest Substring solution and remove the Math.max in the left update.
Find the smallest failing input yourself (hint: try "abba").
Then use the prompt below and compare the AI's explanation with yours.
Restore the fix and add "abba" as a test.
Type QUIZ JAVA to be quizzed on ArrayList vs LinkedList.

blocks.title: Interview line
blocks.text: "Before changing anything I find the smallest failing input and the first wrong variable. Then I ask the AI to explain the cause, and I verify that explanation against my trace."

ai.prompt: I'm debugging a Java sliding-window solution for LeetCode 3 (Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters). Input "abba" returns 3, but the expected answer is 2. Here is my code: [paste code]. First, explain the root cause in one sentence and point to the exact line. Do not give a fix yet. Wait for me to confirm I agree, then suggest the smallest possible change, and finally give me 3 more inputs that would have caught this bug.

interview_qa.q: How do you debug a failing piece of code?
interview_qa.a: I reproduce it with the smallest failing input, trace variables to find the first wrong value, explain the cause in one sentence, make the smallest fix, and add that input as a test so it cannot come back.

interview_qa.q: How do you use AI when debugging?
interview_qa.a: I give it the code, the failing input, expected and actual outputs, and ask for the root cause before any fix. I check its explanation against my own trace and only then apply a minimal change.

takeaways: Give AI the failing input and expected vs actual output.
Ask for the cause before the fix, and verify it.
Remember: in your Interview Coach chat you can type QUIZ JAVA to be quizzed on today's Java topic.

interview_angle.asked_at: Meta's AI-enabled round (debugging existing code), Google's code comprehension pilot, and Amazon/Microsoft behavioural questions
interview_angle.how_it_comes_up: "This test fails — find out why" with existing code, or "Tell me about a hard bug you fixed"
interview_angle.strong_answer: A structured method, the smallest failing input, the one-sentence cause, a minimal fix and a regression test.
interview_angle.pitfalls: Randomly changing code; letting AI rewrite everything; not adding a test for the bug.

glossary.meaning: A technique that keeps a range [left, right] over an array or string and moves its ends instead of recomputing from scratch.
A contiguous run of characters inside a string.
A sliding window whose length stays the same as it moves.
A sliding window that grows and shrinks to stay valid.
Constant cost per operation on average over many operations, even if a few are expensive.
The size of the backing array, which can be larger than the number of elements.
A chain of nodes where each node points to both the previous and next node.
Data stored close together in memory, which the CPU can read much faster.
Content Delivery Network: servers around the world that cache content near users.
A CDN server close to users that serves cached content.
Your own server that holds the original content a CDN copies from.
An HTTP header that tells browsers and CDNs how long a response may be cached.
A test added after fixing a bug, so the same bug cannot quietly return.
